summary: This Standards Track document deprecates two key exchanges for (D)TLS 1.2, finite-field Diffie-Hellman and RSA, and discourages static ECDH cipher suites. It applies only to (D)TLS 1.2. It updates many RFCs, including RFC 5246 and RFC 9325.

plainLanguage.summary: Some old locks have known weaknesses, so builders are told to stop using them.

questions: is rsa key exchange deprecated in tls 1.2
why is ffdhe deprecated in tls 1.2
subtitle: TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 must stop using RSA key exchange and finite-field Diffie-Hellman, and should avoid static ECDH.

tldr.problem: TLS 1.2 and DTLS 1.2 still allow key exchanges with known weaknesses: RSA key exchange, finite-field Diffie-Hellman (static and ephemeral), and static elliptic curve Diffie-Hellman. Attacks on them keep recurring because the countermeasures are hard to implement correctly.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC bans RSA and finite-field DH/DHE cipher suites in (D)TLS 1.2 with MUST NOT, discourages static ECDH and fixed-DH certificates with SHOULD NOT, and has IANA mark the affected registry entries with a D in the Recommended column.
tldr.outcome: Clients must not offer, and servers must not select, the listed cipher suites in (D)TLS 1.2 connections. It updates RFC 9325 and sixteen other RFCs, and leaves TLS 1.3 alone.

today: RFC 10015 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2026 and has not been obsoleted or updated. It updates RFC 9325, RFC 5246 and other RFCs listed in its header.

sections.title: Why These Key Exchanges Are Retired
sections.content:
(D)TLS 1.2 supports several key exchange algorithms: RSA, Diffie-Hellman (DH) over a finite field, and Elliptic Curve Diffie-Hellman (ECDH). DH comes in an ephemeral form, where fresh public keys are sent in the handshake and authenticated by the peer's certificate, and a non-ephemeral form, where a static DH public key sits in the certificate. The ephemeral and non-ephemeral finite-field variants are called DHE and DH; for elliptic curves they are ECDHE and ECDH.

The RFC says non-ephemeral suites are generally not recommended because they lack forward secrecy. Reusing a public key, whether through a non-ephemeral suite or by reusing keys with an ephemeral one, also opens timing side channels. The Raccoon attack does this to finite-field DH, and invalid curve attacks exploit secret reuse in ECDH. Both can be avoided in implementations, but the RFC notes that in practice implementations may fail to do so, given the number and complexity of the mitigations.

The scope is limited to (D)TLS 1.2. (D)TLS 1.0 and TLS 1.1 are already deprecated by RFC 8996, and (D)TLS 1.3 either does not use the affected algorithms or does not share the relevant configuration options. There is no DTLS version 1.1.
sections.plainLanguage: Some of the ways computers agree on a secret code have cracks that clever attackers keep finding. The people who write the rules decided to stop using the leaky ones in the older version of the secure-web protocol.

sections.title: The Problems With FFDHE and RSA
sections.content:
The RFC lists five problems with finite-field ephemeral DH (FFDHE) in (D)TLS 1.2:

  • There is no mechanism for negotiating the group, and some implementations only support small group sizes, which causes interoperability problems.
  • FFDHE groups may have small subgroups, which enables several attacks. A client cannot practically verify a custom group chosen by the server, and cannot fall back to other parameters. Custom groups are widespread, so clients cannot simply reject them.
  • Some operators use 1024-bit groups for wide support. That leaves a small margin against the current discrete log record of 795 bits.
  • A handful of very large computations let an attacker cheaply decrypt a large fraction of traffic that uses particular standardized groups.
  • When secrets are not fully ephemeral, FFDHE suffers from the Raccoon side-channel attack. FFDH is inherently vulnerable unless constant-time mitigations are used.

RSA key exchange has three problems of its own. It offers no forward secrecy, by construction. It may be vulnerable to Bleichenbacher's attack, and variants of that attack keep appearing every few years because the countermeasure is hard to implement correctly. And (D)TLS 1.2 has no convenient domain separation for keys, so one vulnerable endpoint can affect every endpoint that shares the same RSA key.
sections.plainLanguage: Some locks are too small, some are made by the same factory so one picked lock opens many doors, and some leave old messages readable if the key is ever stolen. Those are the problems the rule-writers are fixing.

sections.title: What Is Prohibited and What Is Discouraged
sections.content:
The normative rules are short, and each applies only to (D)TLS 1.2 connections:

  • Non-ephemeral finite-field DH: clients MUST NOT offer and servers MUST NOT select these cipher suites.
  • Ephemeral finite-field DH (FFDHE): clients MUST NOT offer and servers MUST NOT select these cipher suites.
  • RSA key exchange: clients MUST NOT offer and servers MUST NOT select RSA cipher suites. The RFC notes these were already marked as not recommended in the IANA registry.
  • Non-ephemeral ECDH: clients SHOULD NOT offer and servers SHOULD NOT select these. This requirement was already present in RFC 9325.
  • Fixed DH certificates: clients SHOULD NOT use and servers SHOULD NOT accept certificates with fixed DH parameters.

FFDHE cipher suites in (D)TLS 1.3 do not suffer from the problems above, so clients and servers MAY offer them there.
sections.plainLanguage: For three of the risky locks the rule is a firm no. For the ECDH locks and the fixed-key certificates, the rule is a strong please do not.

sections.title: Registry Changes and Updated RFCs
sections.content:
IANA has set the Recommended column to D (deprecated, as explained in RFC 9847) and added this document as a reference for the affected entries. The RFC groups them in tables:

  • Table 1: non-ephemeral DH cipher suites (names starting TLS_DH_), deprecated.
  • Table 2: non-ephemeral ECDH cipher suites, whose use is discouraged. They were previously marked N via RFC 9325 and now get D.
  • Table 3: ephemeral finite-field DH suites (TLS_DHE_* and TLS_PSK_DHE_*), deprecated.
  • Table 4: RSA cipher suites, deprecated.
  • Table 5: four TLS ClientCertificateType identifiers, deprecated.

The document updates RFCs 4162, 4279, 4346, 4785, 5246, 5288, 5289, 5469, 5487, 5932, 6209, 6347, 6367, 6655, 7905, 8422 and 9325 to deprecate or discourage cipher suites that use these key exchanges in (D)TLS 1.2.
sections.plainLanguage: There is a big public list of every lock type. The rule-writers went through it and stamped a warning label on each risky one.

sections.title: Changes to RFC 9325
sections.content:
BCP 195 (RFC 8996 and RFC 9325) holds the current IETF recommendations for users of (D)TLS. This document changes several points in Section 4.1 of RFC 9325 and says every other recommendation in those documents remains valid. The changes are summarised in a table in the RFC.

Non-ephemeral FFDH, ephemeral FFDH and static RSA move from SHOULD NOT to MUST NOT. Non-ephemeral ECDH is unchanged at SHOULD NOT. Fixed DH certificate types, which RFC 9325 left unspecified, become SHOULD NOT.
sections.plainLanguage: An earlier rulebook said please avoid for several of these locks. This note upgrades three of them to a firm no and adds a warning for the fixed-key certificates.

sections.title: Certificate Types Affected
sections.content:
To avoid non-ephemeral DH altogether, the RFC also targets the certificate types that carry a fixed DH key. These are rsa_fixed_dh (3), dss_fixed_dh (4), rsa_fixed_ecdh (65) and ecdsa_fixed_ecdh (66) in the TLS ClientCertificateType registry. Clients SHOULD NOT use and servers SHOULD NOT accept them, and IANA marked them D.

The RFC points out that these values only apply to (D)TLS versions 1.2 and below.
sections.plainLanguage: Some ID cards come with the secret key built in. Because that key never changes, the rule says to stop using those cards.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Non-ephemeral finite-field DH suites and ephemeral key reuse for finite-field DH are prohibited because of the Raccoon attack, which showed that timing side channels in processing TLS premaster secrets may reveal the encrypted premaster secret. Both are already considered bad practice without forward secrecy.

For non-ephemeral ECDH, giving up forward secrecy allows retroactive decryption after a key compromise. It may also enable attacks that exploit key reuse to repeatedly query a secret: invalid curve attacks, side-channel attacks and fault attacks. Such attacks are often implementation-dependent, but the RFC argues that building a system that reuses keys and avoids all of them is difficult in practice, while avoiding key reuse precludes the whole category.

For ephemeral finite-field DH in (D)TLS 1.2, the server chooses the group and custom groups are prevalent. Verifying a group's structure is prohibitively expensive for the client, a safelist of known-good groups is impractical, and the handshake cannot fall back to other parameters. A client that offers these suites therefore cannot complete a handshake with a custom group while ensuring security.
sections.plainLanguage: Reusing the same key is like using one house key for years: if someone copies it, everything is exposed. A fresh key each time avoids that, and checking an unknown lock design is too hard for a visitor to do on the spot.
